utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Good morning, everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Today we have two accused absent, namely, Nikolic and Borovcanin. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic is absent this morning temporarily due to a dental appointment which could not be placed at another time. He will be joining us later, and he has signed the proper waiver form which will be given the Trial Chamber later this morning and the proceedings can continue in this absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Mr. Bourgon, and as far as Mr. Borovcanin is concerned, I understand we have a waiver already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, he already signed a waiver. It was already submitted yesterday, same reasons as Mr. Nikolic, and he will join us later this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, for the record, Prosecution today is represented by Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Amongst the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic and Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Haynes. So, good morning to you, Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are going to continue with your testimony today. I understand from what I have been told that you had reached mainly -- roughly halfway through your direct examination of the witness. You can proceed, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, yesterday you explained the proceedings when an order arrived, the procedure --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown 5D820. Procedure when an order arrived at the 1st Corps of the Krajina. 5D820. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is an order coming from the staff, the Main Staff, 27th February 1994. Could you look at the handwritten note which is on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is this note sent to you; is it directed to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you received an order like this one with a note like that, what did you do, then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, pursuant to this order which arrived at the ops room at the command post of the corps, the duty officer informed the forward command post, which was at a distance from the main command post. And then, since he had been given guidelines from the commander, he followed the normal procedure which was to prepare our own order in a written form to be dispatched to the subordinate units which were involved in the implementation of this order. I informed Colonel Vojnovic, who was my superior about this order. Under normal circles, he would be the one to draft such orders. And, in his absence, which is the case at hand, I prepared our own order to the subordinated units and I returned this to the duty officer who then followed the procedure and forwarded this order to the commander for -- for him to sign it and to dispatch it across all the subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, we were talking about certain goods which were band in the humanitarian convoys, and we spoke about video cameras and photograph cameras. I would now like to talk about radio equipment. What was the situation for radio equipment, radios?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in meantime, could the witness be shown 5D775, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You can see at item 2 that there are certain equipment, radio equipment, which was not authorised. Was there a reason for this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: International organisations in their vehicles had equipment to -- fixed equipment, within the convoy to communicate with their headquarters. So there was no need for any additional equipment, especially in light of the fact that some frequencies of radio devices worked on the frequencies that might have been of use to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D773.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this document, you can see that tents were not lead through, they were held back for some time. Why? Could you let us know why tents could not be transported and brought there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a piece of intelligence, according to which the tents were used not for the civilian population but for the military that was deployed along the route or on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was the situation with the sleeping bags?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you may know, the military used sleeping bags. The civilian population did not need them so much as did members of the enemy military.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D767, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is an authorisation from the Main Staff on the 7th of January, 1993. And what I am interested in is last paragraph of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's also the last paragraph in the English version, at item 3. You can't see the text in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I would like to know is about item 3, one sees that in the Belgrade convoys, mattresses and sleeping bags were not allowed either for Muslims or for Serbs. What was the reason not to allow the distribution of these items either to the Muslims or to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, international organisations, and in this particular case the UNHCR, resorted to various means to do stuff. And in order to pay for the passage of the goods that were not allowed, they would offer the goods to us; for example, mattresses and sleeping bags. But the position was the same across the board, the transport of such goods was not allowed and the distribution of those goods was not allowed either among the enemy side or among our soldiers. It was just an attempt that tried to make it look as goods offered to us in order for us to allow them to transport goods to the other side; although, we had never asked for such goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was the situation for the transport of fuel in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, at 9.20, Accused Nikolic and Pandurevic -- and Borovcanin entered the courtroom. Thank you. You may proceed; and sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was, in general, the situation for the transport of fuel in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transport of fuel should have been organised by special vehicles intended for the transportation of fuel. Very often international organisations used additional jerry cans to transport certain quantities of fuel that they did not need, because their vehicles did not use that particular type of fuel. We tried to analyse the end user -- who the end user of the fuel would be, would it be for the civilian population and for powering some and powering some batteries, or would it be used for the combat and non-combat vehicles of the enemy side. Based on that analysis and the information we had from before as to what had happened from the fuel that managed to pass through and ended up in the enclaves, certain guidelines were provided so that the restriction of the transport of fuel was reduced to a level that might correspond to the requirements of power-generating batteries. The quantities of fuel that might have been used for military purposes were either limited or more often than not totally banned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D816. This is an authorisation for the passage of humanitarian convoys on the 4th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As you can see, it is sent to the 1st Krajina Corps, also.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to see page 5 in B/C/S and page 4 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the middle of the page, you can see note 1. The entry of fuel is not allowed. So I think you have already answered that this situation occurred. You also spoke about the quantities of fuel which were not needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1269.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a conversation -- the summary of a conversation which was intercepted, a summary of an intercept; and we can see in this passage, in this paragraph, that General Milovanovic saying that UNPROFOR is carrying abnormal quantities of fuel into the enclaves. This is on the 19th of August, 1994. Later, when you were at the Main Staff, were there such concerns concerning -- were there such concerns about fuel?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNHCR always tried to have a certain quantity of fuel in their convoys, irrespective of the previous agreements and explanations and refusals. This pointed to the fact that that fuel, and also based on other information, that that fuel was required primarily by the military that was deployed in Gorazde. Throughout all that period, the fuel was always a sticking point, although, General Milovanovic had banned its transport on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say that during all this period fuel was always -- you are talking about which period, precisely?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to 1994 as well as the first half of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown another document with another intercept in 1994. This is 5D1273.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this intercept, we can see that -- well, it's a summary of a conversation on the 5th of October, 1994. You see that humanitarian convoys were allowed to go through, but that convoys with fuel were not authorised. You already spoke a bit about the reasons why fuel was a sticky point. Were there later situations in which certain convoys were allowed to go through but precisely fuel was not allowed to go through?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this document you can see that the fuel is intend for UNPROFOR units and we, as soldiers, on the basis of information, how much which combat vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, what's the problem, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I didn't mean to interrupt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- I just wanted to make a point. The intercepts Ms. Fauveau is using are -- my understanding is that they are from the Croatian forces. I don't know a whole lot about them, frankly, but if she can just identify them as from the Croatian forces as each one so that it's clear on the record. I don't think we are going to have an objection from them. But I think it's important to be able to distinguish these from the ones that we know so much about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's fair enough. And I think Ms. Fauveau would agree to that. Yes, I see her nodding. So let's proceed. Sorry to have interrupted the course of your answer, but I thought it was something directly relating to the answer to all the questions that had been put. So let's proceed. Mr. Kralj, you had just said: "From this document you can see that the fuel is intended for UNPROFOR units, and we as soldiers, on the basis of information, how much, which combat vehicles ..." You can start again, actually, and give your full answer to the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this document you can see that the fuel was intended for the UNPROFOR units, and, as such, it was transported in cisterns. However, the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska had the precise information how many and what kind of combat vehicles, let's say, if we are talking about Gorazde or some other protected area, and which quantities were essential for the normal functioning for a specific period of time. It was not allowed to stockpile excessive supplies for which there was no need, because it was always possible to provide more fuel according to existing procedures for the needs of UNPROFOR. It was often the case that the quantities were enormously high, and this was then reduced down to normal quantities and the excess was banned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you remember whether in 1993 and 1994 there were periods of time during which the movement of convoys was suspended or restricted?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were occasions when the convoys would be suspended without this being announced. This would usually happen because of their security because they had information that some activities would be underway, combat activities, which would not be good for their security or for them -- it would not be good to find themselves in the territory under the control of Republika Srpska. Of course, they did not give any announcements in advance that the convoys would be suspended. I really cannot tell you exactly which periods I am talking about or this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: One very last question with respect to that particular period of 1993 and 1994. Do you know how the Serbian civilian population reacted when seeing these convoys move through, convoys that transported goods for the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we had considerable difficulties with the civilian population, especially close to the line of separation with the other side because they believed that they're not receiving sufficient aid while the other side is receiving too much aid and that it is being used for military purposes. And this sometimes caused incidents at checkpoints or along the routes of the convoys in the immediate vicinity of the line of separation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D787.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to item 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read a paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does it say here that because of the situation you've just outlined, things happened that way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the result of the -- that is the result of the situation. All the military organs of power from the president to the president of the Assembly took the position that the convoys of humanitarian aid should be allowed to pass to the other side without obstruction. And that is why the civilian sector often cooperated with the organs of local power or the police organs which were participating in the escort of these convoys for the purposes of adhering to this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday you stated that around the end of 1994 you arrived at the Main Staff. Could you tell us a little bit more about your duties at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, by coming or being posted on duty at the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, I was appointed and assigned to the duties of interpreter for the English language. My first -- or immediate superior was Colonel Milos Djurdjic, who was performing the functions of the chief of the sector for relations with foreign forces. Since this position began to gain more and more in importance, I was assigned additional duties, and they were to acquaint myself with all procedures relating to cooperation with UNPROFOR, international organisations; and to be ready and trained to assist Colonel Djurdjic in his work with these organisations, and in his absence to be able to prepare the required documents myself and to be able to submit them for processing according to the previously established procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who was the immediate superior of Colonel Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: His immediate superior was General Mladic, who later transferred part of the authorities from the sphere of humanitarian activities to the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What happened when the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, was not present at Crna Rijeka? In such cases, who would deal with humanitarian aid convoys and their movement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that situation, Colonel Djurdjic would consult on the issue of the convoys with General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another intercept coming from the Croatia collection.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D1272. This is dated 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to know whether the situation described here was the same in 1995. Do you know whether there were meetings between representatives of the army of Republika Srpska and representatives of UNPROFOR with respect to the passage of UNPROFOR convoys and all related matters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was the practice in matters of convoy and the passages of these UNHCR and UNPROFOR convoys to meet occasionally and as needed both the chief of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska and in some cases the commander as well; but there was a rule who should meet with whom: the chief of the staff with the Chief of Staff, or others who met at lower levels, most frequently with General Milovanovic at his level.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether in 1995 there was an agreement between the Republika Srpska and UNPROFOR with respect to freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After each meeting they would make an appropriate record of the meeting, we could even say an agreement, stating what the things were agreed on during the meeting. And then, the corps commands were informed about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1404. We only have the English version of this document, 1404. 5D1404.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you explained that you can speak English. When you were at the Main Staff, did you have the opportunity to see this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what this document is about for the accused? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the principles relating to the freedom of movement of UNPROFOR. The document is from the 31st of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 2 of the document. I'd like to see signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise the signature we see on the right-hand side of the document, where we read "HQ SA representative"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Tolimir's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was the procedure required for a -- an UNPROFOR convoy to be able to go through in 1995 when you were at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was as follows: The UNPROFOR convoy would be announced to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska via fax at their office at Pale. The request would be submitted according to the already mentioned principles 48 hours in advance, this would be the regular procedure. The request would be in Serbian and in English. The fax would be operating 24 hours a day, seven days a week, meaning non-stop; and most frequently it would be set to automatic reception. The documents were sorted by Colonel Djurdjic or by myself depending on who was at the office at a given time. It was not possible for the office to be left unattended and that the document on reception -- on receipt could not be sorted, the text compared, the text in Serbian and the text in English would be compared. I emphasize this because I would like to point out that often it was illegible because the communications or the connections were not good, so we had to see what it was about so that the document in the Serbian version could be submitted in the mail for information to General Mladic or General Milovanovic. Sometimes, there was a need for direct telephone communication with the UNPROFOR office in Pale to clarify some questions. When the Serbian version of the UNPROFOR request was harmonised, then Colonel Djurdjic, depending on the time available, would submit the document in the regular post for review, or would ask for permission to go to General Mladic directly with the document or, most, frequently, General Milovanovic. Of course, before that he had to inform about all the previously agreed on and signed on matters which they also were very familiar with themselves because they were monitoring the situation and knew the situation. From what I was able to see, on the top page of the document of the original, there would always be an initial of General Mladic or Milovanovic for this convoy to be approved. If something was disputable or it was not in accordance with the regular procedure, that paragraph would be underlined, and it would be most often stated on the document that the rest would be approved but this paragraph that was disputed would not be approved; and UNPROFOR was asked for additional clarification about the purpose or the intent of the articles that were disputed. Then the approved document -- or, on the basis of that document another document would be drafted and logged at the office of Colonel Djurdjic. And again it would be returned for signature most often to General Milovanovic. And then the approved document would be returned by fax to the UNPROFOR office. Then we would usually make sure by calling that they received the document. That would be the regular procedure. The same document would be presented to the duty operations officer for him to use his communication channels and dispatch it to a specific corps so that it would reach the department which dealt with these matters, or, rather, to reach the checkpoint. That was the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated that when requests from UNPROFOR would arrive and when Colonel Djurdjic dealt with them, these requests were submitted to General Mladic or General Milovanovic. Did it ever happen that these requests were submitted to colonel and then later General Miletic? To your knowledge, did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I know, General Miletic never participated in any decision-making with regard convoys, either with General Milovanovic or General Mladic. This was not his job. He had other things to do. He had other obligations that fell within his purview.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was the situation as for signatures of a document which has already -- which had already been prepared or which already contain the decision taken by General Mladic or General Milovanovic? Did you have an opportunity to bring these documents which were already finalised to General Miletic so that he could sign them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were situations when no higher officers were present to sign everything that had already been agreed upon pursuant to the regular procedure so that the document might be dispatched and the aforementioned activity to be implemented. And in such a situation, Colonel Djurdjic would go to the duty operations officer on the day to see, to get information, rather, whether there was anybody authorised to sign the document so as to enable the document to be implemented and complied with and so that the convoys in question could pass. In very rare cases, I even believe that I once had an opportunity to get information from General Miletic as to who was in a position to sign the document that had already been approved.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Excuse me, I interrupted you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic, in exceptional cases and only if the convoy in question was really important, he could be talked into signing; or he would ask the convoys to wait until the moment the superiors came back, or he had obtained approval from General Milovanovic to let that convoy -- or, rather, to have that document signed. This was not common practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown 5D81 -- 881. 881.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you explain what this document is that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is marked as urgent. It deals with the movement of a British convoy from Kiseljak to Gorazde on the 1st of January, 1994, and back. This is about the supply of fuel which was regulated by the weekly supply plan. It was an urgent document, and in the right-hand side in the top corner of the page the initial is by Colonel Djurdjic, if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the fact that the initials of Colonel Djurdjic, if you're right, are on this document, does that mean that Colonel Djurdjic had approved this convoy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What this means for me is that he had had prior consultations either with General Milovanovic or, exceptionally, with General Tolimir. And since this was about the weekly resupply of fuel and the passage of fuel tanks that had already been planned for, I suppose that it was suggested to him by telephone that he should initial that and to send the whole thing into the procedure. Those are very rare cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D882, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, this is the same type of document, but instead of having initials here you can see handwritten, "Colonel M. Djurdjic." Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I don't want to lose too much time with this document, but is this document the same sort as the one we just saw a while ago?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a similar procedure, but the unit in question is DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... 5D1310.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please have a look at this first page. This document indeed is a self-contained document, and could you tell us what it is, what it represents? Briefly, I don't need a thorough explanation for each convoy, but in general what is this document about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is about the movement of several convoys which had not been approved. A short document had to be sent to the UNPROFOR command stating the number of convoys, the time, what was transported. It was not clear from the request, what the purpose of the goods that were transported was. Additional information was sought, i.e., information was sent back that the convoys were not allowed to pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown -- could the witness be shown the bottom of the page where the signature is?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You can see the name of General Milovanovic, and would you be able to recognise the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letterhead always contained the name of Manojlo Milovanovic, that was as per rules, but this obviously is not his signature. It is possible that the duty officer who was -- or, rather, the person who was the duty operations officer's superior, after a consultation with General Milovanovic, signed this document in order to comply with the procedure of maintaining communication with the UNPROFOR command. I suppose that this is the signature of Pandzic, of Colonel Pandzic, who was often the head duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown the top of the page, a bit higher, item 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just to identify what sort of a convoy we are talking about, convoy from Sarajevo to Kiseljak, number 21-228/02.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could one see now the B/C/S version page 2 and page 3 for the English version. Just at the top, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On this document one can see numbers 22102 -- 21-228/02. This is a request for the convoy from Sarajevo to Kiseljak, and I would like to know if you recognise the initials which are at the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just to be quite sure and clear, what do these initials mean, as they are here, just by the name one can read? Just in a circled lane, the initials in a circle.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that the convoy was not approved. It does say "no" in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you see at the bottom of the page, some handwritten observations. Do you recognise who wrote these handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's page 4 for the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that this was additional information by Colonel Djurdjic at the -- at General Mladic's request as to what had been transported previously by the same people. Some supplies could last indefinitely, and it says here, "Only after seven days."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... be here that this matter of 40 beds is mentioned, which had already been imported on the 19th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be possible to go back both for the B/C/S and English version? Page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Item 1, paragraph 2, in this second paragraph can one indeed find what was said in the handwritten note we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not clear, the same number of soldiers, double the number of beds. The question was raised, why if beds were being replaced, why the old ones were not being returned. And the rest should have lasted seven days as had been agreed before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I simply wish to know whether what can be seen on this document, which has been typed, does it correspond to the handwritten words which one has read before on the request coming from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to you. I would just simply ask if that's the question that's going to be put to the witness, that the witness simply read the handwritten note into the record; and the document that's otherwise translated speaks for itself, and we can resolve this, I think, relatively quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree to that, Ms. Fauveau? I think it's -- it will facilitate our lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Mr. President. Could we go to page 2 in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, could you read the handwritten remark which says, "The 19th February"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "19 February, this is what was imported into Sarajevo: 40 beds, 1 pallet of office supplies, 10 crates of beer, 10 crates of fruit juices ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you please read just after that, if you can read it. Is it legible?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a bit illegible, but it says: "Only after seven days, drinks; and in the meantime they should provide additional information as to who the beds are being transported to." Again illegible, and then it continues: "When they return old ones," and I suppose that this refers to the 40 beds.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go back to page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I don't think you need to read paragraphs 2 and 3 of item 1, but was it the regular procedure to incorporate in this document -- document which was to be sent to UNPROFOR, the notes which were written on the requests?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This note refers to the person who drafted the document, and it was not obligatory to write it in that sense. It did not have to be copied word for word. The document had to be drafted in this sense in order to ask for additional information or say why something has not been approved.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown 5D1316, please. This is another notification concerning convoys which hadn't been approved. And this is dated 29 March 1995 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And for this document, please look at the signature. Do you recognise the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Milovanovic's [Realtime transcript read in error, "Mladic"] signature. And there is also a list of convoys which have not been approved.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the basis of the fact that General Milovanovic signed this document, can you say who decided that these convoys shouldn't be approved or wouldn't be approved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, before you answer the question. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think there is a correction due in the transcript with respect to the date of the document. It's indicated 29th March and the document is dated 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 26th of April. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The references to line 18 of the previous page. Okay. Let's proceed, thank you for that, and it will be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is perfectly right, it's my fault. There is another mistake, also. Page 21, line 21. I don't think the witness spoke about the signature of General Mladic. I will ask him again.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you say who signed this document, witness, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Could you please provide me with the page that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: There is a mistake in the transcript. Could you repeat what you said a while ago, who signed this document, if you please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, the Chief of Staff signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The fact that this document or, let's say that the fact that this document was signed by General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The question is leading, and I would ask my colleague to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hadn't finished my question. Well, I don't know how he can say. The witness was just going to say that this document was signed by General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to the signature on this document, can you say who decided not to approve this convoy? Is it possible to say who took the decision on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, by just inspecting a signature, it is not possible to see who it was who decided for the convoys not to be let through. We he don't know whether it was General Mladic or General Milovanovic. We would have to go back to the beginning, to document number 1, and then at the top of the document we could see who initialed the document and added the word "yes" or "no." In this particular case the word is "no," the convoy is not approved.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 2 of the document. Page 2 in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recognise the initials we see on this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic, you can see "no" and his initial.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us now who decided not to approve this convoy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic made the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time it's convenient --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well now, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown 5D1314. This is a notification dated the 29th of March, 1995, related to UNPROFOR convoys that have been approved. I'd like to show page 2 to the witness in B/C/S, page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, here we see a handwritten comment "yes" encircled and next to that we see two initials. Could you identify these initials?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first initial above is one of General Mladic and the other one underneath is that of General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you provide us an explanation. Do you know why both of them initialed this document? With did these two generals initial this particular document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an exceptional situation when both were in the same office. The document was first looked at by General Mladic, then continuing with his review of the mail, he gave it to General Milovanovic to look at, and then he also put his signature on it in order to let Colonel Djurdjic know that the document has already been shown to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 13 of the document in B/C/S and page 19 in English. Please turn to item 6. We have a detailed list of the cargo transported.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why does this request go into such a level of detail?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this is about is it's the Ukrainian Battalion; and what was required is to state the type of equipment and weaponry that was entering the protected area and whether the quantities noted are for themselves or for someone else. That is why we insisted on this and agreed in advance in order to build confidence and trust between UNPROFOR and the army of Republika Srpska that the entire range of equipment and weaponry and other items be put on the list of items being transported by the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When the Main Staff notified its subordinate units of the cargo transported by authorised convoys, would that part of the text, with a list of cargo transported, would that also be sent to the subordinated units when they were notified of the convoys?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. If there was such information in the request, then in order to prepare and carry out adequate checks, the information would mention item by item specifically the equipment or the articles that were supposed to be in the convoy as in the request.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1315.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you're moving, Ms. Fauveau Ivanovic, can you see the upper part of the B/C/S document. Mr. Kralj, we see here as well the signature of Generals Mladic and Milovanovic? No, I'm asking, whether signature of Mladic and whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The upper signature is the one of General Mladic and the lower one is that of General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is it that reads "yes" with "restriction"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Mladic's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is another notification sent to UNPROFOR listing the convoys that have not been authorised. On the first page we see the signature of General Milovanovic, could the witness be shown page 2 of this document, that would be page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recognise the initials on this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be the initial of Milos Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does that mean that Djurdjic approved or, rather, disapproved the passage of this convoy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The question assumes a fact not in evidence. This witness has said that it could be and not that it is, and so I think the question presupposes that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but he hasn't excluded the possibility either. So assuming that there is that possibility, what would be his answer to the last question, provided my colleagues agree with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think she was asking is it meaning of the "ne."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, yes, yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us what this "ne" means, "ne," this handwritten observation we see here. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states here "ne," "no." Since this is about fuel supplies Colonel Djurdjic had a plan for the fuel supplies which was agreed on earlier. Evidently this was not in accordance with the plan, and in the procedure he consulted his superior who was not physically accessible; and he was given oral agreement that this convoy should not pass. For the purposes of record keeping and for information, he had to place his initials there, perhaps he didn't process his document -- this document further, but without the initials the document could not be passed on for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you document P2454.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2554. This is a notification to subordinated units dated 1st of July, 1995. I'd like to show you page 2 of this document. Could the witness be shown the very bottom of the page, please. That would be page 4 in English. Here we see the name of General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Based on this document, can you ascertain who authorised the convoys listed in this document? A total of eight convoys are listed in the document.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say until I see the number of the convoy and whose initials are at the top of the document. That person would have approved it. All this means here is that this is being submitted for further procedure. It does not mean that General Miletic did or did not approve this request or convoy. The role of General Miletic in this case was just to sign what somebody approved and that should go as written information for the information of the person to whom the document is sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to come back to page 1 of this document, please. At item 2, we see that we have a convoy going from Gorazde through Rogatica, Podromanija, Pale, and Sarajevo; and we see that this convoy has been approved, convoy number 01-007/07. I would like the witness to be shown 5D884. This is a request for approval for convoy 01-007/07 going from Gorazde to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recognise the initials we see on this particular document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initials below are those of General Mladic. The one to the right could be that of General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness again P2554. We've just reviewed the request for approval of the convoy mentioned at item 2 of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Based on your experience, can you tell us whether for each of the convoys listed in this document, a request was needed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would every single request show and bear the approval of the person who had approved the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 1 and paragraphs 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, I don't think the record reflects the witness's answer to the last question. I believe he said "yes" but it's not recorded here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: At line 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, you will just have to ask him again.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: For each one of these individual requests, is it the case that they would bear or show the signature or -- or the decision of the officer who was supposed to approve this particular convoy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, without that it could not be released into the procedure of drafting the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please have a look at convoys 5 and 6, just to get an idea of what it's all about. I can tell you it's -- these are convoys going from Srebrenica to Belgrade and Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But now if we turn to page 2 of the document. Page 3 in English. At the very top of the page we see a note stating that these convoys have been approved with some reservation or subject to some reservation, conditionally. We saw that the document bears the name of General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But, do you know who could have drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That calls for speculation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily, he could answer the question. So Mr. Kralj, if you could answer the question. If you know you know, if you don't you don't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The convoy -- actually this document was drafted by Colonel Djurdjic. It was typed in the sector for typing the material, usually the typists would type that under his control, that would be the original version. Evidently, what we have here is the transmission via encryption.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know how Colonel Djurdjic knew that these convoys number 5 and 6 had been approved conditionally?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjic was an expert, and he monitored the overall situation with the convoys. That word "conditional" is a bit unclear to me, because it was either that it would pass or not pass, if anything were to pass. So I cannot precisely answer what this word "conditionally" means in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would the officer who decided that the convoy was allowed to go through, would that officer also set a number of conditions to be complied with for the convoy to go through?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not familiar with that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1307.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This document was sent to you because we see that it was addressed to Lieutenant-Colonel Kralj, and this document is signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Indic; do you know who is Lieutenant-Colonel Indzic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Indzic was in the group for UNPROFOR at the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the very bottom of the page. In the last paragraph we can see that: "Colonel Lugonja spoke with General Tolimir. The journey is approved. The units need to be notified of it."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who is Colonel Lugonja, do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Lugonja worked at the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I think that in a way he was superior to Lieutenant-Colonel Indzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But why did Colonel Lugonja spoke with General Tolimir, do you know why he did that? General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that there were no other officials who were authorised to approve the convoy, and probably this movement was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The question clearly called for speculation, given the witness's answer it seems readily apparent that he doesn't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Started his answer with the words "I assume ..." So it is to an extent speculation. We can't proceed on the basis of assumptions. So you either move to your next questions, Madam Fauveau, or you clarify some things with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This document also has two initials. Can you identify these initials?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic and General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: One could already see on this document that Colonel Lugonja had informed you that this trip was allowed and proved, so why was it necessary to obtain an authorisation, a written authorisation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not draft a document without a written approval. That was the procedure. Irrespective of any prior oral agreements, a written document had to get to Colonel Djurdjic's desk.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the organs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Pardon the intervention again, Mr. President. Just for the record, I would just like the witness to indicate which of the two signatures on the right-hand side is General Tolimir's and which is General Milovanovic's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could you do that, please, Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The top initial belongs to General Milovanovic and the bottom one to General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In 1995 did the civilian organs and in particular the coordination organ, have some influence on the UNPROFOR convoys?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown an intercept, and would it be possible to go into private session just to identify the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could 5D960 be shown to the witness, please. We do not have a translation in English, but we have prepared a draft translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who is Petko Obucina.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petko Obucina worked in the office of the Vice-president Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Look at this intercept. It seems that Petko Obucina speaks first with General Mladic, and after that, he expressly asks for General Tolimir to be put on the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown a bit lower on the page the contents of this conversation. The fifth line from the bottom, one can see the name of Milos, and the fourth, also, from the bottom; and Srebrenica is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know why Petko Obucina asked to speak to General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Or the fourth line from the bottom, one sees that the commander has approved what was requested, approved the request. Can you read this, can you see this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this context, when the commander is mentioned, who is the commander?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always Mladic, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document 5D961. And this is -- this comes from the same collection of documents and there also is an audio recording of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So here again it's a conversation with Petko Obucina and a non-identified person; but you could see the name Kralj, could it be you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the lower part of the page, the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Your answer was not taken in the transcript for my former question. Could you tell us if the Kralj who was mentioned in this conversation, is it you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Da," that's me. Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, one sees that Petko Obucina says that he's spoken to the General, and Djurdjic asks him which one, and Obucina says, Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At the middle of the page Petko Obucina transmits to Milos a mention according to which the principle chief was saying that at Srebrenica one could enter and go out of the enclave. Did you often have situations like this one when Petko Obucina and other civilian organs transmitted to you, colonel or judge [as interpreted], messages from General Tolimir or from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't happen often. This is the only case that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether in such a situation that Colonel Djurdjic checked what was said by Petko Obucina?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, objection, it's a leading question, and it calls for speculation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment, Ms. Fauveau, or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, no thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't agree with you at all, Mr. Vanderpuye. If he could answer that question, he should do so. So Mr. Kralj, if you could that question, without speculating, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Djurdjic, in this case, went to General Tolimir's office to clarify the situation. Whatever was not covered by papers and approvals could not be sent into the procedure. Very often people in the coordination body were not privy to our further procedures, and they thought that things could be done over the telephone, which was not the case. It just could not be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1280. This is an intercept coming from the Croatian collection. This is a summary of a conversation which took place on the 13th -- of the 30th of June, 1995. The office of General Nicolai, executive office of General Nicolai is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know who was General Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Nicolai was the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR, I believe. Yes, I'm certain he was the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And General Nicolai, apparently, sent a request to General Tolimir, and it's seen between brackets that there is General Mladic mentioned between brackets. Did General Tolimir, about these humanitarian issues and the UNPROFOR convoys, did he replace General Mladic for these matters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir was involved in the procedure to approve convoys and to meet with UNPROFOR on the issue of convoys, and he would be replaced by General Milovanovic. In the absence of General Milovanovic, General Tolimir could also issue approvals; however, the UNPROFOR procedure was as follows: If they had contacted General Tolimir as per the procedure, then they would continue talking to him for any assistance because they already knew him because they had already met with him; and that's why they addressed General Tolimir in the hope that he would be able to assist them, to speed things along. And this case, obviously, is about the transfer of the body of a fallen soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned contacts with UNPROFOR, did you ever take part -- or did you ever attend a meeting with representatives of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning with the commander of the Main Staff, I was at a meeting that took place at Sarajevo airport, and I also participated quite often when Colonel Djurdjic met with the representatives of the UNPROFOR office in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether General Miletic attended the meetings with the members of UNPROFOR? I am speaking of the period going from the 1st of January, 1995 until end of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1306. This document is dated 6 March 1995, and one can read the name of Colonel Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not Colonel Miletic's signature. This is -- it looks like Pandzic's signature to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this document, the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska informs UNPROFOR that General Milovanovic is absent; and, therefore, the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army proposes to postpone the meeting until the return of the general. In the Main Staff, was it decided who could negotiate with UNPROFOR, who was in a position to negotiate or discuss with the representatives of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was decided. Since this involved a commander of the UNPROFOR staff, the normal procedure was that when the UNPROFOR request was discussed, that the meeting would also be attended by the Chief of Staff of the army Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you have any information on this? Did General Mladic request from President Karadzic and from the civilian organs of the government some instructions when he was going to meetings with the representatives of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The normal procedure stipulated for the presidency to be informed about the activities of the Main Staff involving UNPROFOR before a meeting. And after the meeting, appropriate reports were sent to the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document 5D1295. This is a document sent by the general commander Mladic to the president of the Republika Srpska. This is a very short document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We see that General Mladic sends to the president the equipment or documents concerning the meeting of the 19th -- January 19th, 1995 and requests suggestions concerning the position of the delegation. Here, it's a question of freedom of movement. You have already in part answered my question, but did General Mladic -- was he in a position to decide alone with -- without the president on matters as important as freedom of movement of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the freedom of movement for the UNPROFOR is a very broad term. It implied the freedom of movement across the entire territory under the control of the army of Republika Srpska, which required additional positions and involvement on the part of the civilian authorities, the civilian police, and in a way informing the population about UNPROFOR activities. Thus, the issues of such important nature had to be communicated to the president and guidance was sought from him on those matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We have already spoken about fuel matters. I would like to ask you a specific question concerning the fuel for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1276. This is an intercept from the Croatian collection dated 3 January 1995. And this conversation takes place between General Mladic and Svetlana the translator of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the middle of the document one can read that General Mladic said that for Srebrenica, 35 tons in total. This would be enough for five months, should suffice for 5 months. You have already said there were some estimations made of the quantities necessary, but could you explain how and who did these estimations or calculations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done by the competent organs of the technical services together with Colonel Djurdjic based on the number of vehicles, the UNPROFOR activities that took place in Srebrenica, and a proposal would be given to -- for this to be something that would allow for the normal work of the UNPROFOR. And there was also intelligence according to which some of the fuel was shared with the military of the opposing side which was in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: A few questions, a few technical questions I would like to ask you. Were there any problems - I think you already mentioned this - were there any problems when receiving requests from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were technical problems, problems of technical nature, because of the illegibility of the documents which were faxed through. Sometimes the fax would run out of paper, so only one half of the document would go through. That's why additional information would be sought over the telephone in order to complete such incomplete documents. It also happened that UNPROFOR office provided us with roles of fax papers, because they were the ones who spent most of our fax papers, that's why they provided us with supplies to facilitate our communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D834. This is a document from 1994, but what I am interested in is in the third paragraph, one can see: "[In English] From the UNPROFOR command for the former BH is badly planned."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the situation such -- what was the situation in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The coordination on the UNPROFOR side was not good enough. They did not inform us properly about the time of arrivals of their convoys at the inter-points. So it happens that on one day several convoys were supposed to pass through the entry checkpoint. And in view of all the activities that such a checkpoint had to undertake in terms of the controls of the convoys, there were certain problems created by that. Both for those who were involved in the -- in the checks as well as in traffic; in other words, unnecessary confusion and commotion would be created at the checkpoint which resulted in the faster checks, and as a result the checks were not of good quality. In order to avoid such situations, the checkpoints, i.e., the commands of the corps brigades proposed adequate solutions and that was to talk to the UNPROFOR command and draft a joint plan. This would be aimed at convoys moving faster, safer, and easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When the Main Staff informed subordinate units of the passage of convoys, would subordinate units also report to the Main Staff that the convoys had passed through?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a regular procedure to proceed along the line of command announcing to the corps which convoys are approved. And then, in the response or return information, in regular reports, the answer would be provided if the convoy had passed through, if there were any problems in relation to the passage of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1070, please. This is a regular combat report from the Drina Corps dated 4th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At item 3, we have a list of convoys, a rather short list. Is this what you were referring to earlier when you spoke about information provided by subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the answer. They were not getting into details. They would just cite the number of convoys and what you see here, just the basic information. This was enough for us to compile our records and to note down that such and such a convoy had passed through.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you receive more detailed reports related to proposals made by subordinate units to improve the operation of checkpoints or to identify problems?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D847.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday I showed you a similar document, but it dated back to the beginning of 1994. Here we have a document that bears no date, but because of content and since it refers to what happened in 1994, we can come to the conclusion that this document dates from 1994, the beginning of 1995. Did you ever see any such documents at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the document, but Colonel Djurdjevic [as interpreted] had a habit of briefly informing me about documents of this type that he would receive. I am familiar with the contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could page 2 of the document be shown to the witness, please. Page 2 in English, as well. At item (c) this relates to behaviour and abuse of mandate by UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could Colonel Djurdjic have notified his superior, General Mladic, or anyone else at the Main Staff, with respect to that particular section of the report?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the procedure was reverse. All the mail that would arrive at the Main Staff would be submitted for review by the commander or the chief; and in this case the commander or the chief would pass the document -- I mean, they would read it first. More likely that would be the case than General Djurdjic reading it first, and then they would issue the adequate guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 of item (c), in the last sentence of this paragraph, we see that up to 30 transits by convoys and individuals were approved daily. When you were at the Main Staff in 1995, how many requests would you receive on daily basis, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier that it was a skill to take these requests from the fax and to arrange them, because they would be arriving in a period from -- at a certain period we would be receiving 20 to 30 requests via fax on a daily basis, that's why we would to sort them. And it was receiving 24 hours a day, and for 24 hours a day there was the option of disposing of those requests. That was just here. I am not even referring to requests that were sent to other corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know anything about medical evacuations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were requests for evacuation due to health reasons from the enclaves, and the way out was by road or by helicopter. These requests were processed summarily, and those who needed assistance -- to make sure that those who needed assistance would have these requests approved in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you 5D890. This is an authorisation for any medical evacuation from Srebrenica to Sarajevo. The document is dated 21st of March, 1995. Based on your recollection, can you tell us whether during that period and after the 21st of March of any medical evacuations took place from Srebrenica whilst Srebrenica was a protected area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were medical evacuations from Srebrenica. And these were of patients, allegedly civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D894. This relates to another medical evacuation from Srebrenica to Sarajevo. The document is dated 27th of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the third paragraph of this document we can see that 30 civilian patients are being evacuated as part of this medical evacuation. Who was in charge of approving such medical evacuations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All approvals for entry and exits into the enclaves were approved by the Main Staff, by the chief or the commander, the commander or the chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you mention the chief, who is this? Who you are thinking of?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am thinking of the chief of General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1313. Item 3, please. We find the approval of a medical evacuation that has to take place in the period between 28 to 30th of March, 1995. And in order to avoid any misunderstanding, this relates to the 30 patients mentioned in the previous document. Could we now turn to page 4 in Serbian, in the Serbian version of the document, please. That would be page 5 in the English version of the document. Under item 2 of this request, we see that this relates to 30 civilians patients who have to be evacuated out of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recognise the initials underneath the handwritten comment we see at the very top of the page?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Mladic's initial.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Something is handwritten, and we see -- and then rest is illegible. Who is Toso?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why did General Mladic get in touch with General Tolimir and not directly with Milos to deal with the situation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was relevant intelligence that medical evacuations were being used for various diversions or for different purposes, for transport of specific persons or equipment. And there were indications, and this did happen, that these evacuations were always approved in time. And this procedure would then include the service that General Tolimir was dealing with, that he would carry out the required assessments and conduct the appropriate talks with General Djurdjic for purposes of preventing abuses of medical evacuation convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You talked about evacuations by helicopter. Based on your recollection, can you tell us whether in 1995 there were evacuations by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were medical evacuations as well as helicopter trips into protected areas. I am talking about UNPROFOR helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 5D1296. This is a request for approval for a helicopter flight.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown very bottom of the page, the handwritten part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recognise this handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 2 of the document. The very top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does this confirm what you've just said? I am talking about the signature we see here, does this confirm what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is General Mladic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1297. This is document dated 7th of February, 1995. Here we see that General Mladic approved a helicopter mission, but in the first paragraph he talks about frequent requests for helicopter missions and of abuse of this, something that took place in the night between 6th and 7th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you hear about such abuses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, something that I should have asked you earlier on. We see a number here, 06/17-121. Does this number mean something? I am talking about 06, does 06 mean something particular?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in office correspondence, the office that recorded the post separated the list of documents under the number 06, which was something that Colonel Djurdjic maintained for the needs of registering the cooperation with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations.
